title: Classes and objects vs structs

answers: The call consumes the value, so it cannot be used afterwards
The method is static and has no `this`
The method can be called only once per program
writing.exampleCaption: `increment` borrows mutably, `is_full` only reads, and `new` is a plain associated function.
writing.explanation:
A JavaScript class bundles fields, methods and a prototype chain, and every method receives the same mutable `this`. Rust splits the parts. A `struct` declares the fields and their types, and an `impl` block adds functions. There is no constructor keyword: `new` is an ordinary associated function returning `Self`, called as `Counter::new(2)`. There is no inheritance either; shared behaviour comes from traits.

The receiver is the part without a JavaScript equivalent. `fn is_full(&self)` only reads, so it works through a shared reference. `fn increment(&mut self)` changes fields, so the caller needs a `mut` binding and exclusive access for the duration of the call. `fn close(self)` takes ownership: after `wallet.close()` the caller can no longer use `wallet`, which is how Rust says "this object is finished" without a runtime flag.

Fields are private to their module by default. Outside it, `c.count = 99` does not compile unless the field is `pub`, so an invariant such as `count <= limit` is enforced by the methods rather than by convention. Inside the defining module, as in this single-file example, `main` can still read `c.count`.

A struct literal must set every field; there is no `undefined` property. Optional fields are `Option<T>`, and defaults come from `#[derive(Default)]` or an explicit constructor. Printing a struct with `{:?}` needs `#[derive(Debug)]`, and comparing two with `==` needs `PartialEq`.
writing.feedback: `self` by value moves the struct into the method. The second `c.finish()` is E0382, use of a moved value.
writing.question: What does `fn finish(self) -> u32` tell a caller that `fn count(&self) -> u32` does not?

recall.answer: `&self` is a shared reference, so the method may only read fields: E0594, cannot assign to `self.count`. Change the receiver to `&mut self`; callers then need a mutable binding.
recall.question: Why is the assignment rejected?

recall.answer: As an associated function without a receiver in the `impl` block, for example `fn from_text(text: &str) -> Option<Counter>`, called as `Counter::from_text("3")`. `new` is the same kind of function by convention, not a special constructor.
recall.question: How does Rust express a JavaScript `static` method such as `Counter.fromText(text)`?

writing.rule: `&self` reads, `&mut self` modifies and `self` consumes: the receiver tells the caller what a method does to the value.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every case, including withdrawing the exact balance and reading it through `&Wallet`. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: A class becomes a `struct` for the data and an `impl` block for the methods, and each method's receiver says whether it reads, changes or consumes the value.
writing.task: Port the JavaScript `Wallet` class shown at the top of solution.rs: `new`, `deposit`, `withdraw` (which refuses more than the balance and returns `false`), `balance` and `close` (which returns the final balance and ends the wallet). Keep the receivers in the starter: `balance` must work through a shared reference and `close` consumes the wallet. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied methods in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
